poster.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
poster.bookOrigin: Colombian literary context: García Márquez’s Spanish-language novel. The selected first edition was published in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
poster.creator: Iris Pagano
poster.alt: A cream cover with black Spanish title and author blocks above a pale blue ship set in dense branch-like texture, with three black and yellow plant emblems along the foot.
poster.blurb: A blue ship sits among branches instead of open water.

notes.title: The displayed edition
notes.body: Editorial Sudamericana, Buenos Aires, May 1967. Iris Pagano’s first-edition ship cover, reproduced in Biblioteca Nacional Argentina’s exhibition catalogue; distinct from Vicente Rojo’s later 1967 design.

notes.title: Writing and image-making
notes.body: The Biblioteca Nacional Argentina catalogue identifies Iris Pagano’s first-edition cover. The author and designer are separate contributors, and a later familiar cover is not substituted for this object.

notes.title: A visible design relationship
notes.body: The hull’s fine blue grid contrasts with the rough surrounding texture. Three bold black and yellow forms provide a regular lower rhythm.

studyData.intro: A finely drawn blue ship sits in rough vegetation above three bold plant emblems. This is Iris Pagano’s first-edition cover, reproduced in the Biblioteca Nacional Argentina catalogue, rather than the later Vicente Rojo design.

regions.label: A blue vessel without open water
regions.summary: A pale blue ship occupies the middle of the cover, surrounded by irregular grey and dark marks.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A pale blue ship occupies the middle of the cover, surrounded by irregular grey and dark marks. Its structure remains finer and more regular than the surrounding texture.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The unlikely setting creates a tension between a constructed vessel and an enclosing landscape. The cover invites that comparison without illustrating a single documented scene here.

regions.question: What changes when a ship is pictured among branches rather than on a broad sea?

regions.label: A grid describes the hull
regions.summary: Curved horizontal and upright blue lines divide the hull into many small compartments.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Curved horizontal and upright blue lines divide the hull into many small compartments. Pale paper remains visible between those lines.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The grid gives the vessel volume while preserving a light overall tone. Its regular divisions make the ship easier to distinguish from the loose surrounding marks.

regions.question: How does the hull’s repeated structure differ from the texture behind it?

regions.label: Thin lines rise into the forest
regions.summary: Several narrow blue mast and rigging runs extend above the hull.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Several narrow blue mast and rigging runs extend above the hull. One taller slanting run on the right contrasts with the more upright centre.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The thin extensions make the ship taller without adding a heavy block of colour. They weave visually into the surrounding rough texture while keeping a different hue.

regions.question: Which mast is easiest to follow, and what helps it remain continuous to your eye?

regions.label: An irregular enclosure
regions.summary: Grey and dark branch-like marks fill much of the space around the ship.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Grey and dark branch-like marks fill much of the space around the ship. Their density varies and pale gaps interrupt them.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The texture can feel enclosing because it surrounds the vessel on several sides. Its irregularity also lets the ship’s measured lines appear unusually deliberate.

regions.question: Where does the rough texture become dense enough to compete with the ship?

regions.label: Three emblems form a lower rhythm
regions.summary: Three broad black plant-like silhouettes stand along the foot of the image.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Three broad black plant-like silhouettes stand along the foot of the image. Yellow inner leaves and short stems repeat within each shape.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The trio creates a regular lower rhythm beneath an irregular forest. Their bold silhouettes offer a simpler ending to a visually complicated centre.

regions.question: How does the repeated trio change the pace of the cover’s lower edge?

regions.label: Warm interiors in dark shapes
regions.summary: Yellow pointed areas sit inside the three dark plant forms.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Yellow pointed areas sit inside the three dark plant forms. Their narrow stripes and curved bases differ from the pale blue ship.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The warm accent gives the lower edge an independent colour emphasis. Repeating it three times makes the small yellow area feel more substantial.

regions.question: Would one yellow plant have the same balancing effect as three?

regions.label: A plain line above a strange image
regions.summary: Cien años de soledad appears in heavy dark lettering across the upper cover.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Cien años de soledad appears in heavy dark lettering across the upper cover. The line is compact and sits directly above the textured image field.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The clear title provides a straightforward verbal entrance to a less straightforward picture. Its broad horizontal form contrasts with the ship’s tall extensions.

sections.heading: A duration in the title
sections.body: The Spanish title names a hundred years of solitude. The translation identifies the work for English readers while the original wording and its compact line remain visible in the cover.

regions.question: Does the plain lettering make the illustration feel more unusual?

regions.label: An author in a compact upper block
regions.summary: Gabriel García Márquez is set in a dark block above the title.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Gabriel García Márquez is set in a dark block above the title. The two lines occupy the upper right beside the publisher’s smaller block.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The stacked name gives authorship substantial emphasis without requiring another colour. The nearby smaller publisher line creates a second scale of information.

sections.heading: A Colombian work in an Argentine edition
sections.body: García Márquez’s novel belongs to a Colombian literary context, while this first edition was published by Sudamericana in Buenos Aires. The Biblioteca Nacional Argentina catalogue dates the pictured cover to May 1967 and credits Iris Pagano. Work origin and edition location therefore answer different questions.

regions.question: What distinguishes the author’s block from the publisher’s block beside it?

regions.label: Buenos Aires publishing context
regions.summary: Editorial Sudamericana appears in two short dark lines at the upper left.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Editorial Sudamericana appears in two short dark lines at the upper left. The block aligns beside the author name rather than underneath the illustration.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: Placing the imprint near the author gives publishing identity an early place in the reading order. Its smaller size keeps the two roles distinct.

sections.heading: The first cover is a distinct design
sections.body: The catalogue’s caption identifies this ship cover as the first edition, May 1967. It is kept distinct from Vicente Rojo’s later familiar cover. Selecting a particular cover means following the pictured object rather than using a book’s title alone to identify its design.

regions.question: How would the reading order change if the publisher moved to the bottom?

regions.label: The paper remains part of the image
regions.summary: Cream paper shows around the upper lettering and through the thin blue hull lines.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Cream paper shows around the upper lettering and through the thin blue hull lines. The reproduction retains its photographed edge and uneven tone.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The light ground links type and illustration even where their drawing styles differ. Its visible texture also reminds us that this is a reproduced physical cover.

regions.question: Where does paper act as background, and where does it help describe an object?
